draft.title: The impact of a civil wrong
card: A civil wrong, such as negligence or defamation, can affect both sides of a dispute. The effects can reach beyond the court case.
the person who says they were wronged. They may lose money through medical bills, lost wages or repair costs. They may lose health, or have their reputation damaged.
the person or organisation accused of the wrong. If found liable, they may have to pay damages and legal costs. They may also lose standing, meaning the respect others have for them.
Not every effect is a money loss. Harm to health or reputation is real even when no bill has been paid. A court can usually only order money to make up for it.
draft.remember: A civil wrong can cost both sides money, and also health, reputation or standing.

a.q: A gym member in Geelong is hurt by faulty equipment and cannot work for two months. Which impact does lost pay show?
opts: A financial cost to the injured party
A loss of standing for the defendant
A harm to the injured party's reputation
A legal cost paid by the injured party
a.why: Pay the member could not earn is a loss of money, so it is a financial cost to the injured party. It is not a legal cost, which is the cost of running the case, and it has nothing to do with reputation.
a.clue: Think about what the member could not earn while off work.

b.q: A newspaper in Ballarat is found liable for defaming a local chef and must pay damages. Which impact is a loss of standing for the defendant?
opts: Readers trust the newspaper less after the ruling
The newspaper must pay damages to the chef
The chef's restaurant loses customers after the story
The newspaper pays its own lawyers for the case
b.why: Standing is the respect others hold for a person or organisation. Readers trusting the newspaper less is a loss of standing for the defendant. Paying damages is a money cost, and the lost customers are harm to the chef.
b.clue: Standing is about how others see the defendant, not what it pays.

a.best: A financial cost to the injured party

b.best: Readers trust the newspaper less after the ruling

problems.detail: The clue ('Standing is about how others see the defendant, not what it pays') rules out the two money options and points straight at the only option about how others see the newspaper, so it nearly gives the answer away.
